speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: President Halimah is a popular figure who is well-respected in many circles.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: She was also my former Member of Parliament, who worked hard to serve her constituents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the immediate aftermath of announcing this year's Presidential Election as reserved for Malay candidates, the media reports highlighted how the public embraced the move with open arms, welcoming a Malay President after a break of 46 years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yet, as the dust started to settle, it was clear that the public was very divided over this issue.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At public discussion forums, such as the one organised by the Institute of Policy Studies on 8 September, law professors and retired politicians raised legal issues and shared adverse public opinions on the matter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, in the past few days, it seems to me that the top Government leaders have been going into overdrive, trying hard to convince Singaporeans that the Elected Presidency is an integral pillar of Singapore's commitment to multiracialism.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government now appears to be well-aware of the unhappiness on the ground caused by its manoeuvres to install President Halimah.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Neither is it my purpose to go into the legal arguments, some of which have been aired in our Courts in July.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Motion focuses on the Parliamentary debates, and one aspect only of those debates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What did the Government tell Parliament was the basis for counting Reserved Presidential Elections under the hiatus-triggered model, and was what the Government told Parliament accurate?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Did the Government all along make a policy decision itself to count from President Wee Kim Wee?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Did the Government merely use the Attorney-General's Chambers' (AGC's) advice as a cover to avoid full Parliamentary debate on why the count was not starting from President Ong Teng Cheong?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To answer this question, it is necessary to start with what happened in November during the debate on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During that debate on 8 November, the Prime Minister told the House the following: "… the symbolic role of the President is just as important as his custodial role.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As a symbol of the nation, the race of the candidate is relevant.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, while individually, a good candidate of any race will be satisfactory, collectively, over a period of time, we need that mix of Presidents of different races, and the election mechanism must be designed to produce such a mix over time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is what the hiatus-triggered model delivers." "When should the racial provision start counting?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Constitutional Amendment Bill states that the Government should legislate on this point.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That must have been why the Prime Minister sequenced the sentences as he did, that having taken the AGC's advice, the Government was counting the five terms from President Wee Kim Wee.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister did not say that the Government intended to count from President Wee Kim Wee and that the AGC had merely confirmed that it was acceptable to do so.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In a Channel NewsAsia (CNA) report on 8 November, there was a headline which read as follows, reporting on the debate: "Next Presidential Election to be reserved for Malay Candidates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Prime Minister Lee says the Government has taken the Attorney-General's advice that the racial provisions in the review of the Elected Presidency will start counting from Dr Wee Kim Wee." That was the headline.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The impression that it was the AGC which advised the Government to count from President Wee was perpetuated the next day, 9 November, by Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During clarification time, I rose to expressly recall that the Prime Minister had said that the decision to count from Dr Wee Kim Wee was "based on the AGC's advice on how to count the terms".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I asked whether the Government was prepared to publish that advice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo did not reply immediately.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After a Cabinet huddle, Deputy Prime Minister Teo eventually rose and responded as follows: "On the reserved elections and how to count, I would like to confirm that this is indeed the Attorney-General's Chambers' advice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And if not, and you do not think that is correct, I think it is possible if you wish to challenge judicially." Let me repeat what he said. "On the reserved elections and how to count, I would like to confirm that this is indeed the Attorney-General's Chambers' advice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And if not, and you do not think that is correct, I think it is possible if you wish to challenge judicially." Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, any reasonable person hearing those words would assume the following: (a) That the AGC had advised the Government how to count; and (b) That the AGC's advice involved a question of law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Why else would I be asked to challenge it judicially?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As the debate went on, I was asked whether I was suggesting that the Prime Minister had falsely told the House that such was the advice of the AGC.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I repeated that my interest was in asking for the AGC's advice to be published.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Three months later, on 6 February, this House held a Second Reading debate on the Presidential Elections (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What struck me in preparing for the debate was that the Bill contained a new Schedule with a Table, stipulating that the count was to start from President Wee Kim Wee.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It dawned on me then that the Government had simply wanted Parliament to make new law to stipulate that the count should start from President Wee Kim Wee.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Minister Chan further said: "The Government is confident of the advice rendered by the Attorney-General.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We proceeded on that basis during the debates on the constitutional changes in this House.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Prime Minister Lee explained to all why we needed the hiatus-triggered mechanism, and we passed the Constitution (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We are here today to put the nuts and bolts in place for a decision made clear by the Prime Minister during the debates in November.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And we will not go through this again…" He continued: "Ms Lim once again questioned the Attorney-General's advice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If it is the first, then I think Ms Lim, as suggested by Deputy Prime Minister Teo, can challenge this in the Courts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But if it is the second, then I am afraid it is a very serious issue to cast aspersions on the integrity of our Prime Minister." Sir, we should note what happened here.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Instead of confirming that it was the Government who made the decision to count from President Wee, Minister Chan explicitly said that the Government was confident of the AGC's advice and proceeded on that basis to make the Constitutional changes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He said he did not want to reopen the debate on the count from President Wee, even though Parliament was then asked, for the first time, to enact the Table stipulating the count from President Wee.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Here we were debating a law that would practically rewrite history, by deeming President Wee as the first Elected President.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yet, instead of the Government using the opportunity to clarify the matter and any misimpressions created, it chose, instead, to impute sinister intentions to me.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And that was how the Parliamentary debates on the reserved Presidential Elections ended.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In High Court Originating Summons No 495 of 2017, Dr Tan sought a declaration from the Court that the amendment to the Presidential Elections Act in February to count from President Wee Kim Wee was unconstitutional.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In other words, his case was that Parliament had passed an unconstitutional law in February when it legislated the Schedule to the Presidential Elections Act, with the Table to count the hiatus from President Wee.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The basis for this opinion was that one had to read the Constitution in a purposive manner, that is, the Constitution should be interpreted in a way that furthers its purpose.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Since the purpose of the Constitutional amendment was to cure the problem of five Presidential Elections not turning out a candidate from a particular ethnic community, counting from President Wee did not make sense, since he was never elected.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This would mean that it was proper to count only from President Ong Teng Cheong or later.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If that were to be done, this year's Presidential Election would still be open to candidates of all communities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Deputy AG Hri Kumar, a former People's Action Party (PAP) Member of Parliament, represented the Government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He made the following submissions to the Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What the Prime Minister said is that the AG advised that what the Government was proposing to do was legitimate." This is from the Official Court transcript.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Mr Hri Kumar further submitted that the decision on which President to count from was a policy matter for the Government and not a legal question.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He argued that, "the AG was in no position to tell the Government where to start the count from." On 31 July, before the Court of Appeal of five judges, the Deputy AG repeated his position even more vividly.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He submitted that the AGC's advice was "irrelevant".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He also tried to explain away the Prime Minister's speech on taking the AGC's advice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He said: "One should not look at speeches like statutory instruments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister had made it clear from his speech that President Wee was not a popularly elected President, but a President who exercised the powers of an Elected President.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Then he says, fifth term of Elected President.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He was not defining presidency in this context as Elected Presidency." That was Mr Hri Kumar Nair's submission to the Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Was the Deputy AG saying that we should not take the Prime Minister's speech literally but loosely?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Not place too much weight on the terms the Prime Minister used in making a keynote speech to Parliament to amend the Constitution?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Ministers kept consistently referring to the AGC's advice as the basis for the legislative changes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I would like all parties interested to look at the Court transcripts to see how the Courts struggled with trying to make sense of what the Government was saying in Parliament with regard to the AGC's advice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I can only assume that revealing the advice would not be useful to the Government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even if one were to give the benefit of doubt to the Prime Minister to assume that the Prime Minister's speech in November was just ambiguous rather than misleading, it is also deeply troubling that nobody from the front bench sought to correct the impression given.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Ministers must have known that the House understood that the Government was acting on AGC's advice on how to count, that there were legal questions involved.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yet, nobody came out to clarify that, "Hey, actually, it was the Government who decided to count from Wee Kim Wee, it was a policy decision.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, we have sought the AGC's blessing to cover ourselves".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Here we are, debating changes affecting the highest office in the land, yet the Government decides to engage in ambiguous language and red herrings.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We in this House should have been told in no uncertain terms that it was the Government that wanted to count from Wee Kim Wee.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government should have defended its own decision on why counting from President Wee was appropriate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It should not have evaded the debate by using the AGC's advice as a distraction and then gone to Court to say that the AGC's advice was irrelevant.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Did the Government refuse to publish the advice because doing so would have made it clear that the decision to count from President Wee was initiated by the Government and the Government alone?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government's inconsistent explanations would further fuel the suspicions of Singaporeans about the real intention behind the legislative changes that resulted in this year's Presidential Election being a closed one.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When the Prime Minister announced the appointment of the Constitutional Commission to review the Elected Presidency system, he said, our President is the Head of State, he represents all Singaporeans in our multiracial society.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As such, it is important that the minorities have a chance to be elected and that this happens regularly.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In a dialogue session held after the Government released its White Paper, I was asked the following question: when would the circuit breaker to hold the Reserved Election after a racial group has not been represented in Presidential Office after five continuous terms come into effect?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When we put in the Bill, we can say we want it to start from this period.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is … a policy decision…" CNA reported it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal has confirmed that it was for Parliament to decide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She heard that this Judge asked that question; that was said, this was said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why does Ms Lim not read the judgment?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is only one person in this House whom the Courts have held to be misleading Parliament and he is not from the PAP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Only one person, after evidence is heard − Ms Lim knows whom the High Court held was misleading Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I suppose Ms Lim knows all about misleading Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal's judgment makes clear a number of things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members can read the part Ms Lim quoted from the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not see anything that is ambiguous.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The point is this − and we are not changing history here; Ms Lim is a lawyer, she knows this − Dr Wee, in the second term, exercised the powers of an Elected President.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Parliament could have started counting from Dr Wee; could have started counting from an earlier President.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was made very clear that it was a policy decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in the context of that, for example, if we wanted to start from Dr Wee, are there any legal impediments to start counting from Dr Wee?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am just talking about one question amongst many that can arise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are a number of questions that can be asked and there were also provisions relating to minority rights and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I said that we are asking AGC to advise us on a number of questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What Ms Lim is saying is that we are starting to count from here because of AGC's advice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We start counting, we are a careful Government, we make a policy decision, but we take advice to see whether there are any impediments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And this Government, as a rule, generally does not publish legal opinions that it gets.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If it can be done according to the law, we do it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the law has to be changed to achieve policy objectives, we do it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I said it upfront, well before the Parliamentary proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the Court of Appeal said the Prime Minister was very clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What Deputy AG Hri Kumar said in court is: you do not try and take every Member of Parliament's speech and every Minister's speech and then try and interpret it as if it is statutory interpretation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we had a long spiel, totally irrelevant, about the QC's advice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Lim knows what happened to the QC's advice in Court, she carefully omits saying anything about that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we know how QC's advice can be obtained.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What matters is what the Court of Appeal has said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the Court of Appeal has been very clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They said that the Prime Minister has been very clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This argument that it was unconstitutional does not have any leg to stand on, because the Constitution provided for Parliament to legislate, and Parliament legislated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Nobody is suggesting that Dr Wee was elected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is an untruth that is attributed to the proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is suggested is that he was the first person to exercise the powers of an Elected President.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And is there any legal impediment for us to start counting from there?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are questions which others may just decide for themselves.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we will usually ask AGC for advice on these things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that is exactly what − you know if you look at the context − we decide, and we check with AGC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Prime Minister said it, Deputy Prime Minister Teo on second day said it, and Minister Chan said it a few months later.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court of Appeal, as a matter of law, said AGC's advice is irrelevant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: AGC also argued in Court that their advice is irrelevant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because for the legal question of whether a provision is unconstitutional or constitutional − and Ms Lim really should know about this, instead of spending so much time making a point out of nothing − the question before the Court is: this particular provision in the Presidential Elections Act, is that constitutional or unconstitutional?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court has got to look at the constitutional provisions, it has got to look at the provisions in the legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It can have a reference to Parliamentary debates, if the provisions are not clear, and decide how it interprets, which is what the Court of Appeal did.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And in that context, what one party − the Government's lawyers told the Government, or what the other party's lawyers told the other party − Dr Tan Cheng Bock − are completely irrelevant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is a legal argument AGC put forward, and that is a point that the Court of Appeal also makes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that is quite different from the Prime Minister, in Parliament, explaining that: "Look, you know, these are the steps we have taken.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have also taken AGC's advice." He is telling that to the Members.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is the truth, but it is irrelevant as a matter of law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then, we explained it on the ground, district by district.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that we are taking advice on a number of issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am paraphrasing because I do not have it in front of me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why would I go and say it is a policy matter if I thought it was a pure legal issue?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Ms Lim is right, then I was misleading all of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Minister Shanmugam, you have 30 seconds to wrap up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will use up the 30 seconds and sit down.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The next day, Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hian, and subsequently, Minister Chan Chun Sing, took the same positions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If there is a certain legal approach, then we can change the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have got to read whatever statements I have made in the overall context that Parliament is sovereign.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Its will is sovereign − and the real issue is: can we achieve what we want, within the current framework of taking this approach?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or do we need to make some changes?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That means we are now in the fifth term of the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We also have to define the ethnic group of each of the Elected Presidents we have had so far.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is no practical doubt, but as a legal matter, we have to define it".

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The time allowed for the proceedings has expired.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The Question having been proposed at 7.05 pm and the Debate having continued for half an hour, Mr Deputy Speaker adjourned the House without Question put, pursuant to the Standing Order.
